name: George Washington
role: Commander of the Continental Army, first President of the United States (1789-1797)
summary: A Virginia planter and general who presided over the Constitutional Convention and, as president, built a strong, well-financed national government under the Constitution. He warned against party spirit, permanent foreign alliances and the weakening of the Union, held that religion and morality support republican government, and backed liberty of conscience for all. He enslaved people throughout his life, and his will freed those he owned after his wife's death.

property-fundamental.rationale: Describes government's task as maintaining all in the secure and tranquil enjoyment of the rights of person and property; his own landholdings were large.

strong-leader.rationale: Warned that the spirit of party leads people to seek security in one man's absolute power, and that consolidating powers in one hand creates despotism; also left office after two terms.

state-harmful.rationale: Calls a government of vigor, with powers properly distributed, indispensable and the surest guardian of liberty; says liberty is little else than a name where government is too feeble to protect person and property.

limit-guns.rationale: Signed the 1792 Militia Act, which enrolled every free able-bodied white male citizen aged 18 to 45 and required each to provide himself with a musket or firelock.

reviewHistory.rationale: Said a free people ought not only to be armed but disciplined, and wanted a uniform militia plan, so favoured an armed citizenry rather than strict limits.

universal-morality.rationale: Speaks of the immutable principles of private morality and the eternal rules of order and right which Heaven itself has ordained, binding every nation.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Urges discharging debts in peacetime and avoiding the accumulation of debt, not throwing the burden on posterity, and using credit sparingly.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Writes that reason and experience forbid expecting national morality to prevail without religious principle, and calls religion and morality indispensable supports of political prosperity.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Opposed immigrants settling in a body, since they would keep their language, habits and principles, preferring intermixture so that they or their descendants get assimilated to American customs and soon become one people.

national-mission.rationale: Hoped the country would be an example of exalted justice to mankind but urged non-entanglement, not spreading its government abroad.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Signed acts chartering a national bank and creating federal patents for inventors, measures beyond defence, justice and the protection of property.

reviewHistory.rationale: Asked Congress for a national university, a military academy, post roads, boards to promote agriculture with public money, a navy and encouragement of manufactures, so he did not limit government to defence, justice and property.

consent-of-governed.rationale: States that the basis of American political systems is the right of the people to make and alter their constitutions, and calls the government the offspring of the nation's own choice.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Ordered the 1779 Sullivan expedition, an offensive aimed at the total destruction and devastation of the Six Nations' settlements.

separated-powers.rationale: Stresses the necessity of reciprocal checks by dividing and distributing power among different depositaries, and warns that encroachment of one department on another leads to despotism.

head-commands-forces.rationale: As president he called the militia of four states into service on his own proclamation and sent it against the western Pennsylvania insurrection.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Wrote in 1788 that he differed widely from Jefferson and Lafayette on rotation in the presidency, saw no danger of a president perpetuating himself, and saw no propriety in barring the services of the man most capable in an emergency.

reviewHistory.rationale: Declined a third term and wrote his Farewell Address to retire, though the Constitution did not bar a third term; he did not argue for a legal limit.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Told the Quakers that the conscientious scruples of all men should be treated with great delicacy and tenderness, and that laws should be accommodated to them as far as the protection and essential interests of the nation permit.

collective-defense.rationale: Warned against entangling the country in European quarrels through permanent alliances, saying temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies suffice.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Wished his office to be free of party animosities and local prejudices, and in the Farewell Address warned against the spirit of party in elective governments.

patriotic-education.rationale: Asked Congress for a national university to assimilate the principles, opinions and manners of young Americans from every quarter and to teach the science of government to the future guardians of the country's liberties.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: In 1788 he thought a bill of rights nugatory because the people kept all they did not expressly give up, but in his first inaugural (1789) he invited Congress to consider how far the rights of freemen could be impregnably fortified by amendment.

reviewHistory.rationale: Holds that the existing constitution is sacredly obligatory on all until changed by an explicit act of the whole people, and that changes must come by amendment, never by usurpation.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

term-limits.rationale: Opposed rotation in the presidency in 1788, writing that the country should not preclude itself from the services of any man deemed most capable in an emergency.

abolish-ip.rationale: Signed the Patent Act of 1790, which granted inventors the sole and exclusive right to their inventions for up to fourteen years.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Commanded the Continental Army through eight years of war, an armed defence of the independence the colonies had declared.

arms-reduction.rationale: Warned against overgrown military establishments as hostile to republican liberty yet wanted a respectable defensive posture.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on confidential negotiation or discretion in diplomacy, and the statement now asks only whether agreements between governments should ever be secret.

reviewHistory.rationale: Told the House that foreign negotiations require caution and often depend on secrecy, and refused to hand over the Jay Treaty instructions.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Wrote that all possess alike liberty of conscience and immunities of citizenship, and addressed a Jewish congregation as equal citizens.

national-church-status.rationale: Wrote that all in the United States possess alike liberty of conscience and immunities of citizenship, and that toleration is no longer spoken of as the indulgence of one class toward another.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Proclaimed against settlers and armed bands violating treaty lines and Indian lands (e.g., James O'Fallon's Kentucky force) and ordered legal punishment of invaders of Cherokee towns.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Signed the 1791 excise on domestically distilled spirits and then enforced it with the militia against the western Pennsylvania resistance.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Said the Constitution and laws bind until changed by the whole people and that obstructing laws is destructive of liberty.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Signed the Coinage Act of 1792, which set up a national mint and defined the money of account by gold and silver coins of fixed weight and fineness.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: Signed the 1795 act pledging the sinking fund and import duties until the whole of the present debt, foreign and domestic, is fully and completely redeemed.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: His record points both ways: in 1779 he ordered the devastation of the Six Nations' settlements, while as president he issued proclamations against settlers and armed bands violating Indian treaty lands.

no-central-bank.rationale: Signed the act that chartered the Bank of the United States in 1791.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: Ordered that the Sullivan expedition aim at the total destruction and devastation of the Six Nations' settlements and the capture of as many prisoners of every age and sex as possible.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Proclaimed a national day of prayer asking God to promote the knowledge and practice of true religion and virtue and the increase of science among the people.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: Wrote that no member of the convention objected to trial by jury, and that it was left out only because a single mode would clash with the different practices of the states.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: Says it is the true policy of the United States to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world, relying on temporary alliances only for extraordinary emergencies.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Nulled: this id now asks whether social change should respect established institutions (reused 2026-11-10); this answer was to its earlier text, "Social reform should proceed in small steps.", and moved to gradual-change, which now has that text.

reviewHistory.rationale: Urged that changes to government be tested by time, habit and experience rather than mere hypothesis, warning against the spirit of innovation.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Granted that parties may usefully check a government within limits, but held that in governments purely elective the spirit of party is not to be encouraged and should be mitigated by public opinion.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Commanded the armed revolution against British rule rather than limiting opposition to petitions and other legal channels.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Wanted the United States to have as little political connection with foreign nations as possible and to keep out of European quarrels, while hoping it would be an example to mankind.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: Wrote to Lafayette that nations were becoming more humanized and that the benefits of a liberal and free commerce would before long succeed the devastations and horrors of war.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Ratified the Jay Treaty, which referred the St. Croix boundary and British creditors' claims to joint commissions whose awards both governments agreed to treat as final and conclusive.

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: Signed the Naturalization Act of 1795, which required applicants to renounce on oath all allegiance to any foreign prince or state.

notes: On slavery, he was a lifelong slaveholder who wrote in 1786 that he wished to see gradual abolition by legislative authority and would not buy more slaves, and in 1799 freed those he held in his own right (not the dower slaves) at his wife's death. Slavery-specific record, such as the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 and the Naturalization Act of 1790 limited to free white persons, was left null where no statement matches. Several answers rest on one or two passages in Farewell Address and annual messages; the Newburgh Address, Founders Online papers and Jay Treaty text itself were not available to the auditor. Second pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-10): brought up to rules 5. Founders Online refused scripted access (AWS WAF challenge), so letters were read in the public-domain Fitzpatrick and Sparks editions on archive.org, the annual messages in the Gutenberg collection and the Miller Center corpus, and the acts he signed in the Statutes at Large on Wikisource. Answers that cited Wikipedia or mixed his record with his words were re-answered from the record (tariff, bank, excise, militia, neutrality and Thanksgiving proclamations). Searched by theme: government (rotation in office, jury trial, bill of rights, monarchy, civil control of the army), world (alliances, neutrality, arbitration, war, commerce), immigration and naturalization, slavery, Indian policy, religion, debt, money and taxes. His 1788 letter to Lafayette opposing rotation in the presidency replaced the earlier reading of his retirement as a lean against unlimited re-election.
